title: One, two, many: how languages handle number
invitation: See what your language already does with one thing, two things, and more, then compare it with the language you are learning.
summary: Languages do not all divide number the same way. Some make nouns singular or plural. Some also have a dual for exactly two. Others often leave nouns unchanged and let numerals, classifiers, determiners, particles, agreement, or context carry the number.

runtime_copy.correct_fallback: Yep. That number pattern fits here.
runtime_copy.retry_fallback: Not quite. Check what number is meant and where this language marks it, then try again.

blocks.title: Ask three questions
blocks.description: Which number meanings does this language distinguish? Does it have to mark them? Where does the marking show up: the noun, another word, agreement, or just the context?

blocks.text: Do not translate an English plural ending. Learn the number system your target language actually uses. If the noun can stay unchanged, that is a rule too.

Now watch number spread through real noun phrases. In Spanish, for example, el libro nuevo becomes los libros nuevos: the article, noun, and adjective all move together. But la crisis becomes las crisis, so an unchanged noun can still sit inside a plural phrase.
Try a few where there is one defensible answer. Gef skips a question when the language genuinely allows more than one number-marking choice.

blocks.title: Find number in the wild
blocks.description: While you read, spot where the language marks one, two, or more, and where it leaves number unmarked.

blocks.title: You found the system
blocks.description: Number is not a universal suffix. Learn which distinctions your language makes, whether marking is required, and where the grammar puts the evidence.

RULE.es.number.plural_s.summary: For the common Spanish pattern, an unstressed-vowel ending usually takes -s.

tips: Check ending-specific spelling and stress changes instead of adding -es blindly.

RULE.es.number.invariant_nouns.summary: Some Spanish nouns do not visibly change for plural.

RULE.es.number.agreement.summary: Spanish number usually propagates through agreeing words in the noun phrase.
tips: el libro nuevo → los libros nuevos
la casa blanca → las casas blancas
